name: Hibiscus tea
caffeine: None: hibiscus is the dried calyx of roselle, not the tea plant, though a blend may add black tea or other plants.

house.ask: Not printed on the menus: ask at lineup whether the bar keeps hibiscus, hot or iced, which brand, loose or bagged, and the price.

what: Hibiscus tea is a tisane of the dried red calyx of roselle, Hibiscus sabdariffa, the fleshy cup around the seed pod: not the garden flower and not tea. Steeped, it gives a ruby liquid sharp with fruit acids and tasting of cranberry. Mexico drinks it as agua de Jamaica, West Africa as bissap, Egypt as karkadé and Jamaica as sorrel, and on a bar it doubles as a tart, red zero proof base.
taste: Tart and bright, cranberry-sour with a floral thread, and close to sour unsweetened, so most cups want sugar, honey or agave. Boiled hard, it picks up a dry, dusty finish from the seed fragments.

steps: Rinse the dried calyces briefly in cold water to shift dust, and drain them at once.
Weigh 2 to 3 g per 6 to 8 oz for a cup, or about 45 g per litre for a strong batch.
Bring fresh water to the boil; for a concentrate, let it settle just off the boil, near 195F (90C).
Pour it over and steep 5 to 10 minutes for a hot cup, or about 20 minutes off the heat for a concentrate.
Strain without pressing or wringing, which clouds the liquid and leaves grit.
For a batch, sweeten while warm, then chill hard, and taste again cold, because cold flattens sugar.
Iced, shake 5 oz of chilled strong hibiscus with a half ounce each of lime and agave, and pour over ice.
make.ratio: 2 to 3 g per 6 to 8 oz; about 45 g per litre
make.dose: 2 to 3 g calyces per cup; sweetener to taste; lime for iced
make.temp: 195 to 212F (90 to 100C); off the boil keeps the perfume
make.time: 5 to 10 minutes hot; about 20 minutes for a concentrate
make.cup: Warmed glass mug, 8 to 10 oz; iced, a Collins

serve: Hot, it goes in a warmed glass pot or mug, because the colour is half the sale, with sugar or honey beside it and a dish for the bag. Iced, the Library build is shaken with lime and agave and poured into a Collins over ice, with a lime wheel and mint. Pour with care: it reddens anything it touches.
story: Hibiscus is drunk on three continents. Its origin is argued between Sudan and West Africa; China, Sudan and Thailand are the big growers today, and Mexico’s crop is rising. Every culture that grows it drinks it: agua de Jamaica in Mexico, sweet and iced; bissap in West Africa, sometimes with mint and orange blossom water; karkadé in Egypt; sorrel in Jamaica, spiced with ginger and pimento. A guest who knows any of those names already knows the taste.
guest: Hibiscus is a dried red flower calyx rather than tea, so it has no caffeine of its own; it tastes tart, like cranberry, and works hot or over ice.
watch: It stains: the red marks linen, white shirts and anything it touches, so pour with care and wipe the station at once.
A long rolling boil, as some agua de Jamaica recipes use, can add a dry, dusty finish, and wringing adds cloud and grit; strain without pressing.
A guest asking for sorrel may mean this Caribbean hibiscus drink, not the sour green leaf of the kitchen; ask which.
Sweeten an iced batch a shade past correct, because cold flattens sugar on the tongue, and taste it cold before it goes out.

recall.prompt: Hibiscus tea: how is it brewed, and how does the Library build it iced?
recall.answer: Dried calyces steeped in water from just off the boil to a full boil, 5 to 10 minutes for a cup or about 20 for a concentrate, strained without pressing. Iced: 5 oz chilled strong hibiscus, a half ounce each of lime and agave, shaken and poured over ice in a Collins. Tart and cranberry-red.

quiz.q: Which part of which plant goes into hibiscus tea?
options: The petals of the garden hibiscus
The leaf of a red Camellia sinensis
The cut leaf of a South African shrub
The dried red calyx of roselle
quiz.explain: It is Hibiscus sabdariffa, roselle: the fleshy red calyx around the seed pod, dried. The garden flower is grown for show, no tea leaf goes in, and the South African shrub is rooibos.

quiz.q: A guest from Jamaica asks the bar for sorrel. What do they most likely mean?
options: A purée of sour green leaves
A tisane of the sorrel leaf
quiz.explain: In Jamaica, sorrel is the hibiscus calyx steeped with ginger, pimento and spice. The sour green leaf of the kitchen is another plant; sorrel sold dried or as a drink is hibiscus.

quiz.q: Why do some recipes steep hibiscus just off the boil and strain it without pressing?
options: Boiling adds a dusty finish; wringing adds grit
Pressing the seeds releases caffeine into the drink
Boiling water makes the fruit acids taste sweet
Gentler heat stops the drink staining linen
quiz.explain: Colour and tartness leave the calyces fast near 195F (90C). A hard boil drives off the perfume and seed fragments give up tannin; wringing adds cloud and grit.
